subject: exercise-sports-science
title: Energy Systems: Three Systems Sharing One Bout
objectives: Describe the handover in order: all three systems on together, ATP-PC fading as the phosphocreatine store drains, glycolysis peaking as lactate builds, the aerobic system ramping up to dominate
Explain why no energy system ever switches completely off during the bout
State the share of each system at the first seconds, at about 10 seconds, at about 30 seconds and minutes in

definitions.meaning: The three overlapping ways the body resupplies energy during exercise: the ATP-PC system, anaerobic glycolysis and the aerobic system; all three are active from the first second of a bout.
The system that uses the phosphocreatine store to resupply energy fastest; it holds the largest share at 70 percent in the first seconds and fades as the store drains.
A small store in the muscle that fuels the ATP-PC system; it drains within seconds of hard work, which is why the ATP-PC share falls from 70 percent to 35 percent by about 10 seconds.
Breaking down glucose without oxygen to resupply energy; it takes the largest share at 55 percent at about 30 seconds, and lactate builds as it works.
The substance that builds up in the muscle while anaerobic glycolysis holds a large share of the energy supply, as in scene 3 of the animation.
The system that uses oxygen to resupply energy; its share climbs from 10 percent at the start to 75 percent minutes in, so it dominates longer work.
The percentage of the total energy supply provided by one system at a stage of the bout; the three shares always sum to 100 percent and none is ever zero during the bout.

mechanismSteps: All three on together: in the first seconds ATP-PC holds 70 percent, glycolysis 20 percent and the aerobic system 10 percent, so every system contributes from the first second (s1).

The store drains and ATP-PC fades: by about 10 seconds the phosphocreatine store has drained, ATP-PC falls to 35 percent, glycolysis rises to 40 percent and the aerobic share climbs to 25 percent (s2).

Glycolysis peaks as lactate builds: at about 30 seconds glycolysis holds the largest share at 55 percent while lactate builds, the aerobic share reaches 35 percent and ATP-PC is down to 10 percent (s3).
The aerobic system dominates: minutes in, the aerobic system supplies 75 percent, while glycolysis still supplies 20 percent and ATP-PC 5 percent (s4).
workedExample: Read the handover stage by stage. Step 1 (s1): in the first seconds the shares are ATP-PC 70 percent, glycolysis 20 percent and aerobic 10 percent, summing to 100 percent with ATP-PC largest. Step 2 (s2): at about 10 seconds the drained phosphocreatine store drops ATP-PC to 35 percent, glycolysis rises to 40 percent and the aerobic share reaches 25 percent. Step 3 (s3): at about 30 seconds glycolysis peaks at 55 percent as lactate builds, the aerobic share climbs to 35 percent and ATP-PC falls to 10 percent. Step 4 (s4): minutes in the aerobic system dominates at 75 percent, yet glycolysis still supplies 20 percent and ATP-PC 5 percent - at no stage does any share reach zero, so the systems overlap throughout.

trap.misconception: The body uses only one energy system at a time and switches cleanly to the next one when the first runs out.
trap.explanation: The slip: The systems feel sequential because textbooks list them in order and each one dominates at a different stage of the bout, so the handover reads as a clean switch rather than a shifting overlap. The fix: All three systems are active from the first second and overlap throughout the bout; only the largest contributor changes as the bout continues - ATP-PC fades as the phosphocreatine store drains, anaerobic glycolysis peaks as lactate builds, and the aerobic system rises to dominate longer work. In class, replay scene 2: freeze as the phosphocreatine store drains and ask what glycolysis and the aerobic system are doing at that same moment - both shares are growing, which is why the handover can never be a clean switch.
